Big Brother Vumacam

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Johannesburg CBD and its surrounding suburbs have now been turned into a surveillance hub. What price are South Africans willing to pay in return for greater security?

Unique Selling Point:
What is the price that South Africans are willing to pay for security and does this come at the expense of our individual privacy? There has never been such a massive roll-out of security cameras in South Africa as those Vumacam are installing across Johannesburg, in a major plan to link security surveillance across the whole city. The plan is to extend the system to the rest of the country. We get an inside look at how the system works.

Summary:
The Johannesburg CBD and its surrounding suburbs have now been turned into a surveillance hub. On many street corners poles designed to house security cameras are being erected, in readiness to watch over you… it’s for your “security”. But as a resident of the city do you know how much the cameras can see, have you been consulted and are you willing to compromise your privacy by having this big brother's eyes on you?

Further information:
Security company Vumacam has over the past 12 months installed about 900 CCTV cameras in the Northern suburbs of Johannesburg such as Melville, Dunkeld, etc. The Cameras are fitted with License Plate Recognition (LPR) software that will they say help security companies and the SAPS to track down stolen vehicles.

Vumacam is a subsidiary of Vumatel and together with Imfezeko Holdings, an investment company, plan on rolling out 15000 CCTV cameras in the city with ultra high-tech capabilities of capturing footage that they plan to sell to security companies and other third parties. The concerning factor about that is, that there are worries that this is not in line with the POPI Act and rights to privacy for the citizens of the city. According to Ashleigh Parry, Managing director at Vumacam, proper procedures were followed and business entities were consulted before the poles could be erected and that they are well within the bounds of the POPI Act, however the question is, how much public engagement was there, and how did they manage to pop up everywhere without residents knowing about it? Was proper consultation with residents and citizens of Johannesburg entered into and how much control do citizens have over the selling of their data to 3rd party users?

What price are South Africans willing to pay in terms of their privacy for feeling safer on their streets and in their homes? In an age where we give permissions to have our information shared, our cameras on our phones and computers accessed, where we knowingly allow a company like google to track our every move, why should a simple camera on our street be troubling? Even so, internationally studies have shown that widespread use of CCTV does not necessarily cut crime, but rather, crimes is deisplaced to where there are no cameras.

Parry also states that the footage from the cameras will only be sold to credible security companies such as ADT, CAP Security, Beagle Watch, 7 Arrows who are already clients of Vumacam. But this brings into question the legality of selling an individual’s personal information to a third party who hasn't necessary subscribed to their service? Parry also suggests that the success rate of such CCTV cameras is evident in suburbs like Dunkeld where the crime rate has reportedly dropped by 90% and they have had an effective CCTV system going for over 12 years.

Vumacam plans to roll these cameras out to more cities in the country and Cape Town is likely to be their next stop. However, Vumacam says the townships, where crime is more prevalent, will not be getting a roll out of these security cameras as not enough security companies operate in those areas and their business model is based on subscription per data feed and camera.

The question remains however, do we live at a time where one’s right to privacy can be compromised without proper consultation and if so what happens to all the data that is collected about you? If you do not agree or are not even aware of being filmed how do you know for certain what this “Big Brother” does with your data? The fact remains that Vumacams are here and ready to capture your every move, but who protects you from those that claim to be protecting you? Carte Blanche finds out…….

Murray Hunter of Right 2 Know does not believe that proper understanding and execution of the POPI act was adhered to by Vumacam, although they say that they ensured they complied with the act. The problem with the act is that it has not been promulgated yet, and there is only the Information Regulator who is the overseer of the act currently, so the argument is that the act is toothless without proper enforcement. Some argue that by the time the act is enforced it will already be outdated. Murray and R2K are questioning the validity of whether Vumacam, who is not registered as a security company with PSIRA, is able to legally capture and store people's data for security purposes, they have written a formal letter of complaint.

Jane Duncan is an academic, public intellectual and activist in the journalism department at the University of Johannesburg. She has done extensive research into surveillance and its efficacy around the world. Her main concern is the ubiquitous surveillance of citizens and that individual privacy is being lost. These cameras form part of our individual loss of privacy where we are fast losing control of where and how are personal data is used. Research around the worked has shown that CCTV cameras do not necessarily reduce crime and when it does, it means that the crime has just moved into a different area. Jane says that all this collected data is vulnerable to hacking and can be used for foul means.

Ahmor Burger-Smidt, an attorney is very familiar with the POPI Act and has written a book “Commentary on the Protection of Information Act”, she has reservations on how this is compliant with personal privacy and use of data, especially when it is sold on to third party users.

Dunkeld in Johannesburg has used CCTV surveillance for 12 years and are one of the first subscribers to the Vumacam system, the residents association whom we will speak to claim to have had a reduction in crime by 90%.

We speak to the residents of Blairgowrie and get their take on the Vumacams. Blairgowrie as a case study highlights how poles have gone up but with no cameras installed, and only now will there be engagement with the residents with regards to the implementation of the cameras. One question is, once the poles are up, is it not addressing the issue of whether the residents want them or not, after the horse has bolted? Ostensibly the poles had to go up as fast as they did, so that Vumacam's wayleaves with the city didn't run out, but how do the residents feel about the process?

Press Release:


What are South Africans prepared to sacrifice for peace of mind? We live in a global crime hot spot, so how much of our personal privacy do we surrender, to a vast new CCTV network? And with a new network of surveillance cameras rolling out in South Africa, is it possible for hundreds of videos to be monitored 24/7?

Script:


VO: If you live in Johannesburg you may have seen these new landmarks sprouting up all over the suburbs, and wondered what they’re all about. They are hundreds of fibre-linked cameras looking out for crime.//

In this incident in Melville captured on CCTV camera, a man is stalking a woman with a laptop, when he finally grabs the laptop she fights back, he pushes her with the laptop into the getaway vehicle.

LINK: How worried are you about your safety? Concerned enough to have a camera watching over you 24/7? This is a Vuma Cam surveillance camera. There's around 900 of them across suburbs of Johannesburg and more to come.

Ricky: We're installing 15 000 cameras just in the city of Joburg and we think that will extend into pretoria, durban, bloem, cape town.

VO: It’s a 500 Million rand investment for Vumacam. CEO Ricky Croock, has been involved in the private security industry for many years. He says the Melville incident was averted when the vumacam surveillance technology alerted the security company, who stopped the vehicle in minutes and the criminals were detained and handed over to the police.

Ricky: Over the years we looked after our neighborhood, we put out cameras but when perpetrators left that neighborhood they were lost so we thought it would be a great opportunity if you had cameras across the city because then you can track and trace and look after suspects everywhere. Let’s start a platform business where we deploy the cctv cameras and sell the videos at a service fee to multiple security companies

VO: Rob Nichol is head of surveillance at Beagle Watch, a Joburg based security company. They have been using the Vumacam system for a while now.

Rob: There’s two types of cameras which are on the vuma cam poles. We've got the license plate recognition camera which picks up license plates of every vehicle that passes through it.That’s being checked against the unicode or SAPS database and any wanted or stolen vehicle is flagged on our system.The second camera is the overview camera and that picks up movement of cars and pedestrians.

Presenter: But is there someone sitting there watching this one camera the whole time

Rob: We call it black screen technology and what that means is the operator doesn’t see any footage until an alert is generated, he then watches a 9 second clip and he will determine whether he deems it suspicious.

Rob: It’s certain instances like this where people reverse on the right hand side of the road we deem that as suspicious. The number plate hasn’t picked up as wanted or stolen cause it’s already gone past the cameras.

VO: The software also picks up unusual behaviour, such as three people standing too close to a boundary wall or humans carrying large objects, it doesn’t just flag people walking on the street.

Rob: we going to look for the 1 in 1000 incident which the algorithm picks up as unusual.

VO: Bramley Community Policing Forum chairperson Harvey Phalatse, is very eager to engage with Vumacam, as it’s already reducing crime in many suburbs.

Harvey: Cameras as a technology tool are very important,they are very beneficial because right at the beginning you are able to capture the incident which you can utilize either from the justice system but also following up on crime so it helps with the investigation

VO: And beyond just capturing the incident, software has the ability to overlay footage that happens at multiple different times. This case involved a red vehicle, first the software filters out the people, and then the non red cars

Ricky: Out of the 1281 objects 19 of those were red vehicles and in 43 seconds we can get to the exact point of finding out when the incident took place

Rob: What we've seen is that there's been a significant reduction in both contact crimes and house robberies.Those are the ones where cctv plays a significant role.

VO: As significant as they can be in solving crimes, full engagement with communities with regard to their right to privacy, before the installation of the cameras is WHAT concerns Professor of Journalism, at The University of Johannesburg, Jane Duncan.

Jane: I think that people who have not been consulted through their resident associations should have a say as well. They have a right to complain to vuma cam and to the information regulator about the fact that they haven’t been consulted.

Presenter: The poles are already put up and only tonight there is going to be a meeting to alert residents

Ellen: We actually put out a whatsapp to the members of our group so yes people knew there were cameras but maybe they aren’t fully aware of what they were there for

Ricky: We can’t discuss it with every single person but if the full committee believe they don’t want those cameras in their area we will engage with them we want to work with communities and enable communities to get safer

VO: Civil Rights organisation Right 2 Know have serious misgivings as to how these cameras are being rolled out throughout Johannesburg. We met Murray Hunter of Right 2 Know at this street corner, where a Vumacam pole is erected but no cameras are installed yet!

But this is the only footage we have left of our interview with Murray filmed off our mobile camera, because minutes later- inside- our whole crew was robbed at gunpoint- all our equipment was stolen- but thankfully no one was harmed.

We asked Vumacam to analyse our armed robbery, from our mobile camera footage.

Presenter: From where we were filming, out the corner of our eye we could see two gentlemen under a tree. Had there been a live Vumacam camera there, how would it have played out differently?

Ricky: A camera is not a silver bullet it would be part of a full solution. Through the software it would have alerted you as unusual behavior with you filming there. What we're creating is situational awareness to identify what’s happening in our surroundings and alert reaction or saps to investigate further.

What we found is They were actually scouting around the area for quite a long time before you were shooting the interview.What the guys were looking for is to say how many are there, are they armed, do they have security presence with them and what thats looking for is to say we want to go to the easiest target possible

Presenter: What else would have been unusual from what you've seen

Ricky: It normally classifies that theres a person and a person has 2 arms. Now you're carrying a camera on top of you, it saying we've never seen this before and what would happen is the control room would have picked that up as an alert sent out a vehicle, and potentially you would have prevented an incident from taking place

VO: And in our case, number plate recognition software would have identified the license number of the robbers’ getaway vehicle and tracked it across the city, dramatically reducing the time it takes to find the suspect vehicle.//

After recovering from our harrowing ordeal, we met Thami Nkosi of Right 2 Know at the same street corner, this time with added security.

Presenter: So From Right 2 Know you have a problem with the Vumacam CCTV cameras that have been put up all over suburbs in Johannesburg.

Thami: There’s an amount of data that gets generated by these cameras that’s not necessarily going to assist in dealing with crime and for us we feel that if people are monitored in terms of how they move that in itself is an invasion of privacies.


VO: Vumacam say they have a strict access permissions protocol and the footage can only be obtained by the police or relevant authorities with a subpoena, that can help lead to effective prosecution.

Presenter: What about those who are saying crime is a reality and these cameras make us feel safer

Thami: There's data to show that the cameras in itself doesn't detect crime. What they do is displace crime from one area to another.

LINK: The protection of personal information act or POPIA protects your right to privacy and the sharing and selling of personal information to third parties without your consent.

VO: Ahmore Burger-Shmidt is head of data privacy practice at Werksmans and is very familiar with the difficulties surrounding POPIA, which is still to be implemented. So is Vumacam breaking any laws?

Ahmore: In terms of capturing CCTV footage. In SA from a data privacy perspective at this stage no. There is nothing like an absolute right to privacy where a data subject can state i've got an absolute right to privacy and therefore you're not allowed to capture me on any cctv footage

Presenter: Vumacam says they are consulting with various residents associations but in some areas the poles are already up before the meetings are taking place.

Ahmore: From a pure protection of personal information perspective, that specific piece of legislation does not provide for the fact that you need to have public consultation process and run through that prior to capturing the cctv footage.From a pure data protection perspective you've got rights and a vumacam they've got responsibilities

Thami: What we would then suggest that vuma cam does is actually go back because i think it was a rushed process, and seek people's consent. It has dire consequences with regards to how many people are surveilled by the cameras

VO: Vumacam say they have complied with city bylaws and are engaging with the city which still has no CCTV policy. In a written response, the city is aware of Vumacam, but is still seeking legal opinion in terms of participating with them. They encourage private companies to innovate in the fight against crime, but stress the need for balance between citizens’ privacy rights and their rights to a safe and secure living environment.

Jane: All of that should be regulated by city wide policy, such as the one that CT introduced and those policies should be publicly consulted.

VO: So, whether you fear big brother is watching you, or need to feel safer, it looks like the Vumacam surveillance cameras are here to stay.

They are hundreds of fibre-linked cameras looking out for crime.// In this incident in Melville captured on CCTV camera, a man is stalking a woman with a laptop, when he finally grabs the laptop she fights back, he pushes her with the laptop into the getaway vehicle. LINK: How worried are you about your safety? Concerned enough to have a camera watching over you 24/7? This is a Vuma Cam surveillance camera. There's around 900 of them across suburbs of Johannesburg and more to come. Ricky: We're installing 15 000 cameras just in the city of Joburg and we think that will extend into pretoria, durban, bloem, cape town. VO: It’s a 500 Million rand investment for Vumacam. CEO Ricky Croock, has been involved in the private security industry for many years. He says the Melville incident was averted when the vumacam surveillance technology alerted the security company, who stopped the vehicle in minutes and the criminals were detained and handed over to the police. Ricky: Over the years we looked after our neighborhood, we put out cameras but when perpetrators left that neighborhood they were lost so we thought it would be a great opportunity if you had cameras across the city because then you can track and trace and look after suspects everywhere. Let’s start a platform business where we deploy the cctv cameras and sell the videos at a service fee to multiple security companies VO: Rob Nichol is head of surveillance at Beagle Watch, a Joburg based security company. They have been using the Vumacam system for a while now. Rob: There’s two types of cameras which are on the vuma cam poles. We've got the license plate recognition camera which picks up license plates of every vehicle that passes through it.That’s being checked against the unicode or SAPS database and any wanted or stolen vehicle is flagged on our system.The second camera is the overview camera and that picks up movement of cars and pedestrians. Presenter: But is there someone sitting there watching this one camera the whole time Rob: We call it black screen technology and what that means is the operator doesn’t see any footage until an alert is generated, he then watches a 9 second clip and he will determine whether he deems it suspicious. Rob: It’s certain instances like this where people reverse on the right hand side of the road we deem that as suspicious. The number plate hasn’t picked up as wanted or stolen cause it’s already gone past the cameras. VO: The software also picks up unusual behaviour, such as three people standing too close to a boundary wall or humans carrying large objects, it doesn’t just flag people walking on the street. Rob: we going to look for the 1 in 1000 incident which the algorithm picks up as unusual. VO: Bramley Community Policing Forum chairperson Harvey Phalatse, is very eager to engage with Vumacam, as it’s already reducing crime in many suburbs. Harvey: Cameras as a technology tool are very important,they are very beneficial because right at the beginning you are able to capture the incident which you can utilize either from the justice system but also following up on crime so it helps with the investigation VO: And beyond just capturing the incident, software has the ability to overlay footage that happens at multiple different times. This case involved a red vehicle, first the software filters out the people, and then the non red cars Ricky: Out of the 1281 objects 19 of those were red vehicles and in 43 seconds we can get to the exact point of finding out when the incident took place Rob: What we've seen is that there's been a significant reduction in both contact crimes and house robberies.Those are the ones where cctv plays a significant role. VO: As significant as they can be in solving crimes, full engagement with communities with regard to their right to privacy, before the installation of the cameras is WHAT concerns Professor of Journalism, at The University of Johannesburg, Jane Duncan. Jane: I think that people who have not been consulted through their resident associations should have a say as well. They have a right to complain to vuma cam and to the information regulator about the fact that they haven’t been consulted. Presenter: The poles are already put up and only tonight there is going to be a meeting to alert residents Ellen: We actually put out a whatsapp to the members of our group so yes people knew there were cameras but maybe they aren’t fully aware of what they were there for Ricky: We can’t discuss it with every single person but if the full committee believe they don’t want those cameras in their area we will engage with them we want to work with communities and enable communities to get safer VO: Civil Rights organisation Right 2 Know have serious misgivings as to how these cameras are being rolled out throughout Johannesburg. We met Murray Hunter of Right 2 Know at this street corner, where a Vumacam pole is erected but no cameras are installed yet! But this is the only footage we have left of our interview with Murray filmed off our mobile camera, because minutes later- inside- our whole crew was robbed at gunpoint- all our equipment was stolen- but thankfully no one was harmed. We asked Vumacam to analyse our armed robbery, from our mobile camera footage. Presenter: From where we were filming, out the corner of our eye we could see two gentlemen under a tree. Had there been a live Vumacam camera there, how would it have played out differently? Ricky: A camera is not a silver bullet it would be part of a full solution. Through the software it would have alerted you as unusual behavior with you filming there. What we're creating is situational awareness to identify what’s happening in our surroundings and alert reaction or saps to investigate further. What we found is They were actually scouting around the area for quite a long time before you were shooting the interview.What the guys were looking for is to say how many are there, are they armed, do they have security presence with them and what thats looking for is to say we want to go to the easiest target possible Presenter: What else would have been unusual from what you've seen Ricky: It normally classifies that theres a person and a person has 2 arms. Now you're carrying a camera on top of you, it saying we've never seen this before and what would happen is the control room would have picked that up as an alert sent out a vehicle, and potentially you would have prevented an incident from taking place VO: And in our case, number plate recognition software would have identified the license number of the robbers’ getaway vehicle and tracked it across the city, dramatically reducing the time it takes to find the suspect vehicle.// After recovering from our harrowing ordeal, we met Thami Nkosi of Right 2 Know at the same street corner, this time with added security. Presenter: So From Right 2 Know you have a problem with the Vumacam CCTV cameras that have been put up all over suburbs in Johannesburg. Thami: There’s an amount of data that gets generated by these cameras that’s not necessarily going to assist in dealing with crime and for us we feel that if people are monitored in terms of how they move that in itself is an invasion of privacies. VO: Vumacam say they have a strict access permissions protocol and the footage can only be obtained by the police or relevant authorities with a subpoena, that can help lead to effective prosecution. Presenter: What about those who are saying crime is a reality and these cameras make us feel safer Thami: There's data to show that the cameras in itself doesn't detect crime. What they do is displace crime from one area to another. LINK: The protection of personal information act or POPIA protects your right to privacy and the sharing and selling of personal information to third parties without your consent. VO: Ahmore Burger-Shmidt is head of data privacy practice at Werksmans and is very familiar with the difficulties surrounding POPIA, which is still to be implemented. So is Vumacam breaking any laws? Ahmore: In terms of capturing CCTV footage. In SA from a data privacy perspective at this stage no. There is nothing like an absolute right to privacy where a data subject can state i've got an absolute right to privacy and therefore you're not allowed to capture me on any cctv footage Presenter: Vumacam says they are consulting with various residents associations but in some areas the poles are already up before the meetings are taking place. Ahmore: From a pure protection of personal information perspective, that specific piece of legislation does not provide for the fact that you need to have public consultation process and run through that prior to capturing the cctv footage.From a pure data protection perspective you've got rights and a vumacam they've got responsibilities Thami: What we would then suggest that vuma cam does is actually go back because i think it was a rushed process, and seek people's consent. It has dire consequences with regards to how many people are surveilled by the cameras VO: Vumacam say they have complied with city bylaws and are engaging with the city which still has no CCTV policy. In a written response, the city is aware of Vumacam, but is still seeking legal opinion in terms of participating with them. They encourage private companies to innovate in the fight against crime, but stress the need for balance between citizens’ privacy rights and their rights to a safe and secure living environment. Jane: All of that should be regulated by city wide policy, such as the one that CT introduced and those policies should be publicly consulted. VO: So, whether you fear big brother is watching you, or need to feel safer, it looks like the Vumacam surveillance cameras are here to stay.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The Johannesburg CBD and its surrounding suburbs have now been turned into a surveillance hub. What price are South Africans willing to pay in return for greater security?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: What is the price that South Africans are willing to pay for security and does this come at the expense of our individual privacy? There has never been such a massive roll-out of security cameras in South Africa as those Vumacam are installing across Johannesburg, in a major plan to link security surveillance across the whole city. The plan is to extend the system to the rest of the country. We get an inside look at how the system works.
metadata.Summary: The Johannesburg CBD and its surrounding suburbs have now been turned into a surveillance hub. On many street corners poles designed to house security cameras are being erected, in readiness to watch over you… it’s for your “security”. But as a resident of the city do you know how much the cameras can see, have you been consulted and are you willing to compromise your privacy by having this big brother's eyes on you?
metadata.Further information: Security company Vumacam has over the past 12 months installed about 900 CCTV cameras in the Northern suburbs of Johannesburg such as Melville, Dunkeld, etc. The Cameras are fitted with License Plate Recognition (LPR) software that will they say help security companies and the SAPS to track down stolen vehicles. Vumacam is a subsidiary of Vumatel and together with Imfezeko Holdings, an investment company, plan on rolling out 15000 CCTV cameras in the city with ultra high-tech capabilities of capturing footage that they plan to sell to security companies and other third parties. The concerning factor about that is, that there are worries that this is not in line with the POPI Act and rights to privacy for the citizens of the city. According to Ashleigh Parry, Managing director at Vumacam, proper procedures were followed and business entities were consulted before the poles could be erected and that they are well within the bounds of the POPI Act, however the question is, how much public engagement was there, and how did they manage to pop up everywhere without residents knowing about it? Was proper consultation with residents and citizens of Johannesburg entered into and how much control do citizens have over the selling of their data to 3rd party users? What price are South Africans willing to pay in terms of their privacy for feeling safer on their streets and in their homes? In an age where we give permissions to have our information shared, our cameras on our phones and computers accessed, where we knowingly allow a company like google to track our every move, why should a simple camera on our street be troubling? Even so, internationally studies have shown that widespread use of CCTV does not necessarily cut crime, but rather, crimes is deisplaced to where there are no cameras. Parry also states that the footage from the cameras will only be sold to credible security companies such as ADT, CAP Security, Beagle Watch, 7 Arrows who are already clients of Vumacam. But this brings into question the legality of selling an individual’s personal information to a third party who hasn't necessary subscribed to their service? Parry also suggests that the success rate of such CCTV cameras is evident in suburbs like Dunkeld where the crime rate has reportedly dropped by 90% and they have had an effective CCTV system going for over 12 years. Vumacam plans to roll these cameras out to more cities in the country and Cape Town is likely to be their next stop. However, Vumacam says the townships, where crime is more prevalent, will not be getting a roll out of these security cameras as not enough security companies operate in those areas and their business model is based on subscription per data feed and camera. The question remains however, do we live at a time where one’s right to privacy can be compromised without proper consultation and if so what happens to all the data that is collected about you? If you do not agree or are not even aware of being filmed how do you know for certain what this “Big Brother” does with your data? The fact remains that Vumacams are here and ready to capture your every move, but who protects you from those that claim to be protecting you? Carte Blanche finds out……. Murray Hunter of Right 2 Know does not believe that proper understanding and execution of the POPI act was adhered to by Vumacam, although they say that they ensured they complied with the act. The problem with the act is that it has not been promulgated yet, and there is only the Information Regulator who is the overseer of the act currently, so the argument is that the act is toothless without proper enforcement. Some argue that by the time the act is enforced it will already be outdated. Murray and R2K are questioning the validity of whether Vumacam, who is not registered as a security company with PSIRA, is able to legally capture and store people's data for security purposes, they have written a formal letter of complaint. Jane Duncan is an academic, public intellectual and activist in the journalism department at the University of Johannesburg. She has done extensive research into surveillance and its efficacy around the world. Her main concern is the ubiquitous surveillance of citizens and that individual privacy is being lost. These cameras form part of our individual loss of privacy where we are fast losing control of where and how are personal data is used. Research around the worked has shown that CCTV cameras do not necessarily reduce crime and when it does, it means that the crime has just moved into a different area. Jane says that all this collected data is vulnerable to hacking and can be used for foul means. Ahmor Burger-Smidt, an attorney is very familiar with the POPI Act and has written a book “Commentary on the Protection of Information Act”, she has reservations on how this is compliant with personal privacy and use of data, especially when it is sold on to third party users. Dunkeld in Johannesburg has used CCTV surveillance for 12 years and are one of the first subscribers to the Vumacam system, the residents association whom we will speak to claim to have had a reduction in crime by 90%. We speak to the residents of Blairgowrie and get their take on the Vumacams. Blairgowrie as a case study highlights how poles have gone up but with no cameras installed, and only now will there be engagement with the residents with regards to the implementation of the cameras. One question is, once the poles are up, is it not addressing the issue of whether the residents want them or not, after the horse has bolted? Ostensibly the poles had to go up as fast as they did, so that Vumacam's wayleaves with the city didn't run out, but how do the residents feel about the process?
